annotations.text: Counter at 1440 — a second design, not a reflow

THE TWO-DESIGNS LAW, APPLIED

The house rule for the staff app is that 820px is a SWITCH between two designs. It holds here, and for a sharper reason: the desktop customer is a DIFFERENT PERSON. A bursar, a procurement officer, a contractor's office — someone with a keyboard, a printer and an approval to justify.

So the desktop is not the phone stretched. It earns its width three ways:

1. The account never leaves the screen. Balance, terms and remaining limit sit in the chrome on every page.
2. The catalogue sits BESIDE the order. On the phone, checking your order means leaving the catalogue; here the total moves as you type.
3. The statement gets its real columns — date, reference, detail, charge, payment, balance — and becomes a document somebody can print and file.

Same tokens, same ledger row, same one-action law. Body stays 15px: this is a customer, not a staff console, and nothing here is worth cramming.

WHAT THE THIRD TILE IS FOR

The phone shows two figures: what you owe, what your limit is. The desktop adds a third — what you have bought this year.

It is the only figure on the surface that is not about money owed, and it is there on purpose. A customer looking at 31,480,000 across 34 orders is looking at the case for asking you for better terms — and at the reason it would be tedious to start again somewhere else.

One strip, hairline dividers, no per-tile borders. Borrowed from the staff console because that part was already right.

THE ORDER PANE IS THE WHOLE ARGUMENT FOR DESKTOP

Every row carries its own stepper, so building a twenty-line order is twenty taps in one place rather than twenty round trips through an item screen.

The advice block rides in the pane, where the total is, so "you have no nails on this order" is read at the moment the number is being judged.

Out-of-stock keeps its row and offers "Tell me when it lands" rather than vanishing. A catalogue that hides what it hasn't got teaches customers to look elsewhere first.

THE GATE IS A DOOR, NOT A WALL

Everything in this product sits behind four figures typed on a phone, so the PIN screen decides whether the portal is used at all.

It goes on WhatsApp, not SMS — that channel already exists in the shop, it costs nothing per message, and it is where these customers already are.

Four things the screen owes the person holding it: which number it went to (so a wrong number is caught here, not after three failed tries), how long it lasts, when they may ask for another, and a plain warning that nobody from the shop will ever ring and ask for it.

No fake keyboard is drawn. The real one renders on top, and a painted one reads as a toy.

A FAILURE NAMES ITSELF — IN INK

The house rule is that no failure may be silent: say what went wrong and how to fix it. So the wrong-PIN screen says which thing failed, how many tries remain, that the lock is fifteen minutes, and that the PIN already sent is still good for six and a half.

AND IT IS NOT RED. Oxide on this surface means money owed and nothing else — that is the whole value of having one colour with one meaning on a screen full of figures. An error marked in oxide would make "you owe" and "you mistyped" the same colour.

So the error is ink, in words, on the warm ground, inside a firm rule, directly above the boxes it is about. Placement and wording carry it. If that turns out to be too quiet in a real yard in real sunlight, the fix is a heavier rule or a larger mark — not spending the money colour.

A DOCUMENT, NOT A SCREEN

Charge and payment get their own columns here. The phone had to merge them into one signed column to fit; at this width the merge is a loss, because a bursar reconciles by reading DOWN a column.

The head block carries what a printed statement carries: who the account is, the terms, the limit, and the balance due — so a print-out is complete without the chrome around it.

Still no accent. The three actions are outlined. Nothing on this page acts on money.
Counter — a design language for the client side

WHAT THIS SURFACE IS

The staff app is a dense work console: steel chrome, 13px type, a hundred figures a screen. It is an instrument.

This is not that. This is the shop's counter, open at 22:00, and its whole job is TRUST — that the price you were quoted in July is the price you get in September, that your balance is not a surprise, and that nothing was hidden from you.

So the language is a well-printed statement of account, not an app: warm paper, hairlines, square corners, real typographic hierarchy, and figures that line up in a column.

Built from the ground up. It shares no tokens with index.html — deliberately, so a customer can never mistake this screen for a staff screen.

FOLLOWING AN ORDER, HONESTLY

The ladder is the app's own order stages in the customer's words: sent, confirmed, getting your goods, ready, on the way, invoiced.

TWO RULES DO THE WORK.

A stage that has not happened carries NO DATE. The books cannot derive when a lorry will leave, so the screen does not invent it — a promised day that slips costs more trust than a blank one ever did.

And it says WHICH LINE is holding things up, per item, because an order is not one thing. "The ridge caps are being collected today" is the honest version of a progress bar.

What it never says is WHERE they are being collected from. This is the single most tempting place in the whole product to name a supplier, and the language has nowhere to put one.

THE SYSTEM

Ground #F4F1EA warm linen · Paper #FFFFFF · Ink #1A1714 warm near-black · Second #6B635A · Meta #9A9187 · Rule #E3DDD3 · Firm rule #C7BFB2

Two accents, one meaning each, matched in lightness and chroma:
   #14594A verdigris — exactly two jobs: THE one filled action, and links. Nothing else. Not "good", not "in stock", not a payment received — those are ink, and the words carry them.
   #9B3A22 oxide — money owed. Nothing else, ever. Not a button, and not "out of stock".

The single tinted ground in the system is the advice block, which is why it reads as advice rather than decoration.

Type: Newsreader for every figure and display line (a printed-statement serif with real numerals); Public Sans for the interface. Not Inter, not Roboto, and deliberately not the staff app's Fraunces.

Ramp 11 / 13 / 15 body / 17 / 22 / 34 / 44.
Space 4 8 12 16 20 24 32 40. Radius 4 on controls, ZERO on sheets — paper has square corners. Tap 44 minimum, and that includes back arrows and the account chip.

Depth is hairlines. One shadow in the whole system: the basket bar, because it genuinely floats.

THE ONE DEVICE: the ledger row

No cards. No coloured left borders. Every list in this language is the same row — name and its basis on the left, figure right-aligned in tabular numerals, a hairline between, a FIRMER rule under a total.

That single device carries the catalogue, the basket, the order history and the statement, on the phone and at 1440 alike. Four screens, one vocabulary, and it is exactly how a paper statement already works — which is the point: the customer has read this document before.

THE WORKFLOW LAW

One screen, one question, one action.

· The screen title IS the question it answers.
· Exactly one FILLED verdigris action, pinned at the bottom in the thumb, on every screen. Zero is allowed (see the Statement); two is a bug. Secondary acts are outlined in ink, never in the accent.
· Ordering is four named steps — Browse · How many · Check · Send — and the step line is drawn ONLY inside that flow.
· The customer never types a price, a code, or an address they have already given.

DERIVED, NEVER INVENTED — and the basis is SHOWN

The house rule says every figure comes from the books. This surface adds the harder half: the customer must be able to redo the arithmetic.

So the catalogue says 48,500 per sheet AND 51,000 loose, because 48,500 is the bundle price and a customer buying six sheets would otherwise have been quoted one figure and charged another. The nails say 1,120 at 8 a sheet AND about 11.2kg at 100 nails to the kg, because they are priced by weight and ordered by count. The over-limit line names the 1,240,000 already owed rather than quietly assuming zero.

Every one of those was wrong in the first draft, and each was wrong in the same way: the figure was right and its basis was invisible.

WHERE THE PRICE GATE SITS

Sign in carries no price at all, and offers the public catalogue by name: "Browse what we stock — names and photographs only. Prices are for account holders."

Everything from screen 3 onwards shows money, because by then we know exactly who is reading. And the figure is THEIRS — held from the last time we quoted them — so a leaked screenshot is one customer's number, not the price book.

No screen in this language has a place to put a supplier's name. That is a constraint of the design, not only of the data.

THE LINE BECOMES A LIST

The green block on screen 5 is the whole commercial argument in one component: "140 sheets takes about 1,120 roofing nails at 8 a sheet."

A supplier sells a line. This turns the line into a LIST — and a list is the thing one supplier cannot fill. It is the only tinted ground in the system, which is why it reads as advice.

Its Add button is OUTLINED, not verdigris. It is a real act, but it is not the act this screen is for, and two accent buttons competing for one thumb is how a screen stops having a primary action.

NO ACCENT ON THIS SCREEN

A statement is read, not acted on, so both buttons are outlined and the accent budget goes unspent. That is deliberate, not an oversight.

The closing figure is oxide because it is money owed. The footnote invites a customer to challenge a line before it becomes a dispute — the staff app already refuses to hide a disagreement between the debt log and the balance, and this is the customer-facing half of that same rule.
Not enough is an answer

A NEW ACCOUNT IS NOT A BROKEN ONE

The house rule: a strip reading 0, 0, 0 makes a working app look broken. Each tile says what it is WAITING FOR instead.

So day one does not show a 0 balance — it says "Nothing outstanding", and names the day the account was opened. Terms and limit ARE shown, because they are true from the first minute and they are the whole reason to have an account.

The long trading name in the chrome is deliberate: "Ssekitoleko Hardware" is the case the house truncation rule exists for, and it is here so the guard can be seen working rather than assumed.

AN EMPTY SEARCH IS A SALE

The public catalogue already refuses to say a flat "No products found" — it names WHICH cause, aisle or search, because the way out differs. The same rule here, and then one step further.

"We do not list it" is the single most valuable thing a customer can tell this shop. It is a demand signal, it is free, and the sourcing side already knows how to turn it into a product. So the accent on this screen is not "search again" — it is "Ask us to find gypsum board", with the honest promise a price and a lead time will come back.

The line about nine of the last ten is a claim the shop must actually be able to make. If it cannot, cut it — do not soften it.

THE ONE TRUE ROW

An empty statement still has an opening balance and a date, and both are facts. They stay.

No accent, exactly as on the full statement — a screen with nothing to act on must not grow a button to look finished.

The footnote offers to carry over trading history from before the account existed. That is not politeness: a customer who has bought from you for six years and sees a statement starting last Tuesday reads the portal as a downgrade.

EVERYTHING ASKED FOR IS NOW DRAWN

Forty artboards across six pages, and the arithmetic agrees across all of them.

ONE JOB runs end to end for the school: quotation QT-0417 at 19,112,640 before VAT, LPO/KPSS/2026/118 raised against it, the purlins chased then cancelled, DN-2419 counted two ridge caps short and a cement bag burst, 16,978,595 invoiced as INV-2402, the top-up Okello James approved invoiced as INV-2441 at 3,698,120, and 12,000,000 received on 30 October leaving 8,676,715 open.

A SECOND runs for the trade customer: order 2341 at 7,821,040, delivered on two lorries, invoiced twice — 7,239,040 and 582,000 — at a price that did not move between them.

Five states were argued down as reflows and later drawn. All five earned a design. The rule holds; it cannot be applied to a screen that does not exist yet.

What is NOT here is the build: no screen in this canvas is wired to anything, and the sample figures are realistic but invented.
If Counter is wrong, these are the other two

Both are drawn low-fi on purpose — they are here to settle a direction, not to be admired.

B · SHOPFRONT is the familiar one: cards, photo tiles, a bottom tab bar, the shape of every retail app your customers already use. Cheapest to get right, and nobody needs teaching. The cost is that it reads as a SHOP — the price becomes the hero, which invites the comparison you are trying not to invite, and the balance and terms become one card among cards.

C · CONSOLE hands the customer the staff app's own vocabulary. Zero new tokens, one system to maintain, and dense tables genuinely suit an institutional buyer. The cost is that it reads cold and administrative to a fundi standing in a yard, and a customer shown the staff chrome will assume they are seeing staff data.

Counter costs the most to build. It is the only one of the three whose shape argues that you are an account, not a price list.
The LPO path — where the price gate does not apply

THE ONE PLACE YOUR PRICES LEAVE THE BUILDING

Every other screen in this product keeps a price behind a verified login and shows a figure that is only that account's. An institutional quotation cannot do that. A school, an NGO or a district needs an itemised document, with unit prices, to put beside two other quotations. That is the procedure, and refusing it loses the work.

So do not pretend the gate holds here. Protect the margin with the things that actually protect it:

A VALIDITY DATE, stated twice and counted down. Fourteen days. After that you re-quote at the day's prices, and the document says so plainly rather than as small print. In a market where cement and steel move on the exchange rate, that single field is the difference between honouring a quote and eating one.

THE BASKET, NOT THE LINE. Delivery included, VAT shown, the whole job priced. A rival undercutting line three has still not quoted the job.

THE RELATIONSHIP. Terms, the promise not to substitute a make without asking, and a named person to ring. None of those appear on a price list.

WHAT A UGANDAN INSTITUTIONAL QUOTATION MUST CARRY

This is not a styled invoice. It is a procurement document, and a missing field gets it set aside rather than queried:

· Both TINs, and both addresses.
· A quotation number and a date, and the person it is addressed to by name and office.
· Unit, quantity, unit price and amount per line — no bundling, because the comparison is done line by line.
· VAT shown separately at 18%, never folded into the price.
· THE AMOUNT IN WORDS. It reads as a formality and it is not: it is what a cheque and an approval memo are written from.
· Terms, a validity date, and room for a signature and stamp.

The TINs and the shop address are left in brackets because they are yours and I do not have them. Everything else is drawn.

A CANCELLED ORDER IS A TRUST SCREEN

This is the screen a customer remembers. So it answers the three questions in order, and none of them is "sorry".

WHO cancelled it, and WHEN. Here it was the customer, at their word, after the shop rang — so both parties are named. A screen that says only "cancelled" invites the customer to assume you dropped them.

WHY, in the words a person would use: the valves could not be got at the price quoted, the only ones available were a different make and dearer, and the shop does not swap a make or lift a price without asking. That sentence is the entire argument for buying from you rather than from whoever answers the phone.

WHAT IT COST: nothing. Charged to your account, 0, under the firm rule and in full ink. What it WOULD have come to is kept, greyed, because a customer re-quoting wants to compare.

Then a way forward, and it is the accent. A dead end with no action is how an order becomes a lost customer.

The reason block is ink on the warm ground, not oxide — nothing is owed here, and oxide means money owed.

AN EXPIRY IS A CONVERSATION, NOT A DEAD END

The fourteen days are what protect the margin, so the screen has to honour them out loud: "those prices are no longer ours to give, and we will not pretend they are."

Then it does the useful thing. It says WHAT ACTUALLY MOVED — two lines of five, named, each carrying "was 48,500" beside today's figure, and the difference on the total. A customer who can see that three of their five lines have not moved in three weeks is looking at evidence that you price honestly, not at a shop that put its prices up because it could.

AND IT IS NOT A RE-QUOTE. A reading off the price registry is derived and fair to show; an offer is a document with a number, a signature and a fresh fourteen days. The screen says which of the two it is, and the accent is "Ask for a new quotation" — nothing re-quotes itself.
One account, several people, different powers

WHY THIS IS NOT A SETTINGS PAGE

A school, an NGO or a contractor is never one person. Somebody raises the order, somebody else approves it, and a third person stands at the gate when the lorry arrives. Give them one shared login and you get the worst of both: the storekeeper can see the negotiated rates, and nobody can prove who ordered what.

So the list is a CONTROL, and the screen says what the shop does with it rather than leaving it as configuration:

· An order over the approval figure does not reach the shop at all until the approver has said yes, on their own phone.
· An LPO signed by somebody not on the list is not accepted. If the signatory changes, it changes here first. That is the cheapest fraud control in the whole product.
· Removing somebody stops them seeing anything from that minute — and does NOT remove what they already ordered, which stays on the account under their name.

THE GATE, WORKING INSIDE AN ACCOUNT

Wasswa Peter receives goods and signs the delivery note. He sees no prices at all.

That is the same rule as the front door, one level in: a person needs what their job needs and no more. A storekeeper does not need the school's negotiated rates to count forty bags of cement against a note — and a storekeeper who has them is the likeliest route by which a rival learns what you charge this school.

It is also the answer to the objection that gating prices is unfriendly. It is not about trust. Sarah sees every figure. Peter has a different job.

THE APPROVER GETS A REASON, NOT JUST A FIGURE

The note from the person who raised it — "the term starts on the 14th and the carpenters want the purlins on site by Friday" — is the most important element on the screen. An approver handed a bare total rings back to ask why, and the order sits for two days.

Every line is shown, not three of five with a total. This is an approval: the whole list is the thing being approved.

Two acts, and only one is the accent. Approve sends it; sending it back to Sarah with a note is outlined, because the screen exists to get a decision, not to make refusing easy.

And the honest line at the foot: nothing reaches the shop until you approve it. Nothing sends itself, and the customer's own staff are no exception.

THE SCREEN WITH NO MONEY ON IT

Every other surface in this product is built around a figure. This one has none, and that is the test of whether the language generalises: the COUNT becomes the figure. Same serif, same tabular numerals, same right-hand column — 240, 46, 19.2, 40. Nothing else changed.

What the storekeeper is given is exactly what the job needs. What is meant to be on the lorry, what he counted, and what is short. The 46 sits where the money would be, and the two short are named in ink rather than hidden in a total.

THE TIMBER IS LISTED THOUGH IT IS NOT COMING. "Named rather than dropped" is a house rule and this is the case it was written for: a line silently missing from a delivery screen leaves a man standing at a gate waiting for a lorry that was cancelled a week ago.

And the screen says its own boundary out loud: you are signing for the count, this shows no prices, signing agrees to none. What is short reaches the shop and the bursar the moment he signs — not through him.

CHARGED FOR WHAT CAME, AND NOTHING ELSE

This is the same job as the quotation, the LPO and the delivery note, and it is where the whole canvas closes:

   supplied        14,388,640
   not supplied     4,724,000
                   ——————————
   the quotation   19,112,640

The purlins were cancelled because only 3m lengths could be got and the customer said not to substitute. Two ridge caps were short on the lorry and the storekeeper signed for 46. Neither is on the invoice, and the footnote does that subtraction where the customer can see it rather than leaving them to find it.

THE INVOICED FIGURE IS INK, NOT OXIDE. Oxide appears on exactly two screens in this product — Your account and the Statement — because that is where a balance lives. What an order was invoiced at is a record; whether it is owed is the statement's question. One colour, one meaning, and it does not wander.

The accent is the way forward: price the purlins again today. A part-supplied order with no next step is a customer going to find the timber somewhere else.

THE PROBLEM, NAMED BEFORE IT BECOMES A CANCELLATION

This is order 2367 a week before the purlins were cancelled, and it is the moment the desktop earns its width: the LADDER and the LINE HOLDING IT UP are read together, in one glance. On the phone you scroll from one to the other and have to remember.

So the screen says which line is the problem, why (the 4m length is short in the market this week), what we are doing about it, and the promise that matters -- we will not put a 3m length on the lorry instead without being told to.

A customer who learns on the 26th is a customer who can decide. A customer who learns on delivery day is a customer who has lost a week of carpenters.

And the rail still refuses to name a delivery date. No date is shown until the lorry is loaded, and the rail says so rather than leaving a blank.

WHAT THE WIDTH ACTUALLY BUYS

On the phone, the part-supplied order had to compress ordered, delivered and short into a line of small text under the item name, and the figure in the money column was what WOULD have been charged -- so the column did not sum.

Here they are three columns of their own, and the last column is what is CHARGED. It sums: 11,640,000 + 1,012,000 + 176,640 + 0 + 1,560,000 = 14,388,640. A bursar reconciling this against a delivery note and an invoice can add it down and get the invoice total, which is the whole job of the screen.

That is the test of a desktop design in this system: not "does it fill 1440" but "is there a column set the phone could not carry".

A FULLY CANCELLED ORDER IS THIS SAME SCREEN, with every line at 0 delivered and an invoice of 0. It is not drawn separately because it would be this artboard with different numbers -- and drawing it would break the rule the rest of this page is built on.

POWERS BECOME A MATRIX

On the phone this had to be a sentence per person, and a sentence cannot be compared. Here it is a grid, and the thing you are meant to notice is a ROW OF DASHES: Wasswa Peter sees no prices, raises nothing, approves nothing, signs nothing. He receives goods.

A matrix makes an anomaly visible in a way prose never does. If somebody has a tick in the approvals column who should not, this is the screen where it is caught.

The three blocks underneath are the same three rules as the phone, laid across rather than down -- and the last line is there because the dashes will be read as distrust by somebody, and they should not be.

The ticks are drawn marks at stroke 1.8, not glyphs and never emoji, so they hold up at any zoom and print black.

THE THREE I REFUSED, AND WHAT THEY TURNED OUT TO BE

These were argued down as reflows — a desktop screen that adds no column, no second pane and no new act is the phone in a wider box. The owner asked for them anyway, and drawing them properly proved that call wrong on two of the three.

CANCELLED IN FULL. I said it was the order-record artboard with zeroes. It is not: at this width the price WE QUOTED and the only price TO BE HAD sit side by side as figures — 96,000 against 118,000 — so the reason for the cancellation is arithmetic a customer can check rather than a sentence they have to take. That is a column pair the phone cannot carry.

NOTHING MATCHED. I said an empty search was a pane going empty, not a screen. That was the finding, not the objection: the order pane stays full beside it, still adding to 14,432,640, and the sourcing ask becomes a real form — what, how much, by when — instead of a second screen. A failure one pane wide is a better design than a failure a screen wide, and it had to be drawn to be seen.

A NIL STATEMENT. Here the original call mostly holds — it is the statement artboard with no rows. But the point it makes is not nothing: a board or an auditor asks for exactly this at year end, and a screen saying "nothing here" is not the same object as a DOCUMENT saying "this statement is complete for these dates", with a signature block and a period you can change.

The rule stands. It was applied too early, on three screens that had not been drawn yet.

IT EARNED ONE, AND FOR A REASON I DID NOT EXPECT

The argument against was that a man at a gate holds a phone. That is still true, and it is not the point: at a DESK the job is different. A phone counts one lorry. A desk reconciles a month — which arrived, which are signed, which went short, and whether a lorry that is not on the list should be turned away. That rail is the first thing the width buys, and it cannot exist on the phone at all.

SHORT AND DAMAGED STOP BEING ONE THING. The phone had one state per line and had to call a burst cement bag "short", which it is not. Short never arrived. Damaged arrived and cannot be used. They are different arguments and they settle differently — one against the shop's count, one against the driver — and conflating them is where delivery disputes actually start. Two columns fix that, and two columns need a desk.

AND THE CONSTRAINT HOLDS HARDER HERE. A 1440 screen full of columns and not one of them is money: a grep of the body finds no comma-grouped figure and no currency word anywhere. Better still, HIS NAVIGATION HAS ONE ITEM. No account, no order builder, no quotations, no statement. The price gate is not a rule applied to this page — it is the shape of the page.

Four for four on drawing rather than arguing.

THE PORTAL SHOWS A PAYMENT. IT DOES NOT TAKE ONE.

That line has been structural since the first migration — there is no checkout anywhere in this product and nothing to attach one to. So a payment screen is not "pay now"; it is the moment a payment the customer already made BECOMES VISIBLE.

Which is worth more than it sounds. Today a bursar sends a transfer, or a fundi hands cash to a driver, and then has no proof it was recorded until the next time they ask. This screen is that proof, with a receipt number they can keep.

THE LEDGER DOING WHAT IT IS FOR. Owed before, this payment, still due — three rows and a firm rule, and a figure visibly moving. It is the same row component as the catalogue and the statement, carrying the one thing those cannot: a change.

COLOUR. The 12,000,000 is INK: a payment is not money owed. The 4,978,595 beneath it IS money owed, so it takes oxide — which makes this the fifth screen in the product to carry the colour, and the rule that put it there is unchanged. Leading with oxide on a screen that says "we received" would have been the easy mistake.

A PART PAYMENT, deliberately. Institutions pay in tranches, and a receipt that can only say "paid in full" is a receipt for a customer who does not exist here. It also lets the screen name the invoice it was put against and how much of it is still open.

No accent: a receipt is read, as a statement is. And the honest line at the foot is the one that earns trust — if you paid something that is not here, tell us rather than assume it will appear.

FIVE FOR FIVE

Drawing it found the gain, and the gain was not the one I would have guessed.

A receipt at this width is a DOCUMENT — the third in the product after the quotation and the statement, and an accounts office files all three. Both TINs, the amount in words, who paid and who recorded it, a signature block.

But the real find is ALLOCATION. A payment is not a figure, it is a figure PUT SOMEWHERE, and at 1440 you can show which invoices it went on and what each has left: 12,000,000 onto INV-2402, nothing onto INV-2441, 8,676,715 still open across the two. The phone could only name one invoice and a rule.

AND THE RULE ITSELF IS ON THE PAGE: oldest invoice first, in full, before anything touches the next — unless you say otherwise when you pay, and then we do what you said and write it here. A payment quietly put against the wrong invoice is how an account stops being trusted, and the fix is to publish the rule rather than to be careful about it.

Drawing this also forced a correction to the phone receipt, which had been showing one invoice on an account that has two. It now reads 20,676,715 owed before, 8,676,715 still due, and names the untouched invoice rather than leaving it out.

Oxide on the closing figure, ink on the amount received. Fifth and sixth screens to carry the colour, same rule.

A SWITCH LABELLED ONLY WITH ITS OWN NAME IS A SWITCH NOBODY THINKS ABOUT

So every power on this screen states its CONSEQUENCE in the line beneath it, in the shop's own words:

· See prices — "she will see every price on this account, including what the school negotiated".
· Sign the LPO — "we refuse an LPO signed by anybody without this. Turning it on is telling us her signature counts."
· Approve — "one approver is usually right; two who both think the other looked is not."

AND PRICES START OFF. That is the load-bearing default in the whole product. The person being added here is a storekeeper at a second block; the restrictive default means somebody has to make a deliberate decision to hand out the school's rates, rather than getting them by filling in a form quickly.

The grant is then read back as ONE SENTENCE before it is granted — she will receive goods and sign for them, see no prices, raise no orders, approve nothing — because a column of switches is a thing people scan and a sentence is a thing they check.

Raising orders says it needs prices on. A power that silently depends on another is how a permissions screen starts lying.

"NOT APPROVED" IS USELESS TO THE PERSON WHO HAS TO FIX IT

The design job on this screen is to get a REASON out of an approver in one tap, because the alternative is an order that bounces back with nothing on it and a phone call that happens two days later.

So: the usual reasons as chips, then room to say the real thing — "Sarah, drop the wheelbarrows for now, we can do those next term. The rest is fine, send it again." That note is the entire value of the screen, and the order's figure stays on it so he is not writing blind.

Dropping the wheelbarrows takes it to 2,394,000, which is still over the threshold — so it comes back to him. The loop is honest about itself.

THE THIRD LINE MATTERS MOST: nothing reaches the shop meanwhile. They have not seen this order and will not until he approves one. A customer's internal disagreement is not the shop's business, and the screen says so.

"Go back and approve it instead" sits under the accent, unstyled. The screen exists to get a decision, not to make refusing the easy path.

A SHORT THAT IS QUIETLY COMPLETED IS WORSE THAN ONE THAT IS NOT

If the last 12 sheets simply appear, a customer cannot tell a late delivery from a forgotten one, and has nothing to point at when the invoice looks odd. So both lorries are named — DN-2377 with 128 of 140 and a reason, DN-2384 with the last 12 — and the order says out loud that nothing is now outstanding.

TWO INVOICES FOR ONE ORDER, and that is the principle rather than an accident: you are charged for goods when they reach you and not before. 7,239,040 on the 15th for what the lorry actually carried, 582,000 on the 17th for the sheets. They come to 7,821,040, which is the figure agreed on the 13th.

AND THE PRICE DID NOT MOVE BETWEEN THE LORRIES. The sheets went on at the 48,500 held from July, two days later, in a market where that figure moves. A delay of ours is not a reason to re-price a customer — and stating it on the screen is worth more than being quietly decent about it.

No accent. It is a record, as the statement and the receipt are.
Shopfront, built properly — the direction not taken

SAME DATA, SAME MOMENTS, DIFFERENT LANGUAGE

Nakato Grace, the same 1,240,000 owed against the same 2,000,000 limit, the same products at the same prices, the same basket at 7,718,000. Only the language changes, because a comparison that changes anything else is not a comparison.

And it is built to WIN, not to lose. A rigged set where only the favourite gets a case made for it is worth nothing.

THE SYSTEM. Figtree throughout, one family, weights doing the work — no serif, because Shopfront has no interest in looking like a document. The house oxide #B23A26 as a brand colour spent GENEROUSLY, where Counter rations it. Cards at radius 14 with soft shadows, pills at 999, a four-tab bar, photos leading every product. Money is bold sans, not tabular serif: a price tag rather than a statement line.

It is a good design. That is the point of drawing it.

WHERE SHOPFRONT BEATS COUNTER, AND IT IS NOT CLOSE

THE TIER. Counter says "48,500 per sheet, 51,000 loose" and makes the customer do the comparison. Shopfront strikes through 51,000, shows 48,500, and puts "Save 2,500" in a badge. A customer understands the second one without reading it. Retail spent twenty years learning that and this direction inherits it for free.

BOUGHT TOGETHER. The product_links ratio lands perfectly in a card idiom — two thumbnails, the arithmetic underneath, one button that adds both for 719,040. Counter's advice block is more explanatory; this is more likely to be tapped.

OUT OF STOCK keeps its card at reduced opacity with a "Back in 2 days" pill and a dead Add button. That reads faster than a greyed figure in a ledger row.

If the job were selling more per basket to customers who already trust you, this direction would win it.

WHERE IT COSTS YOU, AND WHY COUNTER WAS CHOSEN

THE PRICE BECOMES THE HERO. Every tile on the Shop screen leads with a figure in 18px extrabold. That is what a shop does — and it invites exactly the line-by-line comparison the whole strategy is built to avoid. Counter puts the figure right-aligned in a ledger row where it reads as a fact about an account, not a tag on a shelf.

THE BALANCE BECOMES A CARD AMONG CARDS. On Home it is well made and it is scrolled past, between a brand header and four quick-action tiles. On Counter it is 44px of the screen and the first thing read. The thing that actually holds a customer is the thing Shopfront ranks fourth.

THE IDIOM FIGHTS THE PRODUCT. A cart with a checkout button on a portal that takes no money has to be talked out of what it looks like — "No payment is taken here" sits under a button whose entire visual grammar says payment is taken here.

AND THE STATEMENT STRAINS. Cards cannot carry a running balance column. Each row states its own balance and the eye cannot add down them. A bursar cannot reconcile this against a bank statement, which is the one job the document exists for.

THE VERDICT, HAVING BUILT BOTH

Shopfront is the better SHOP. Counter is the better ACCOUNT. The question was never which is prettier — it is which job the portal is for.

The strategy settled that: the portal exists so a customer sees their own price, their own balance and their own terms, and finds it tedious to start again elsewhere. That is an account. A customer who thinks of this as a shop compares prices; a customer who thinks of it as their account compares nothing.

WHAT TO STEAL. Three things from this page belong in Counter and cost it nothing:

· The struck-through loose price with a saving stated, instead of a basis line the customer has to work out.
· "Bought together" as one button that adds the whole ratio, not a row per item.
· Keeping an out-of-stock line visible with a "tell me when it lands" act rather than a grey figure.

That is what exploring a rejected direction is for.

DIRECTION B IS NOW BUILT OUT

This low-fi sketch was enough to settle a direction. It was not enough to judge one — see the Shopfront page for the same five moments drawn properly, with the same data, and an honest account of the three things it does better than Counter.
Console — the house system, handed to the customer

NOTHING HERE IS INVENTED

This direction is different in kind from the other two. Counter and Shopfront are design languages somebody had to make up. THIS ONE ALREADY EXISTS: every token on these five screens is lifted verbatim from .claude/skills/ow-design — the steel ground #E9EBED, the navy 44px bar, the oxide accent, Inter and Archivo Black and IBM Plex Mono, the 2x2 metric strip with hairline dividers and no per-tile borders, the 34px panel header, the 44px tap floor, the filled-active tab.

Even the rules are obeyed: the accent appears exactly ONCE per screen, good is verdigris, caution is amber, bad is crimson and there is no fourth.

So the proposition is not aesthetic, it is economic. ONE design system. One set of tokens, one set of tests, one thing to keep consistent. Every hour spent on the staff app improves the customer app for nothing, and the staff can support a customer over the phone because they are looking at the same screen.

That is a serious argument and it deserved to be drawn rather than dismissed in a sentence.

WHERE CONSOLE WINS OUTRIGHT

THE STATEMENT. This is not close. A ledger with date, entry, amount and running balance in IBM Plex Mono, tabular figures aligning down four columns on a 390px screen — Counter needed a wider gutter and a serif to do the same job, and Shopfront could not do it at all. The console was BUILT to draw money in columns and it shows.

THE PRICE LIST. Dense rows with a right-aligned mono figure is the correct shape for a list somebody scans for one number. It fits more lines above the fold than either rival.

THE METRIC STRIP. Owed, limit left, terms, orders — four figures read at once, in a component that already exists and is already tested. Counter spends a whole screen getting to three of those.

An institutional buyer, at a desk, reconciling — this is the direction they would choose.

WHERE IT COSTS YOU, AND IT IS ONE THING

THE NAVY BAR IS THE STAFF SIGNAL. It is the single strongest visual fact in the staff app, and putting it above a customer's balance destroys the only boundary between "our instrument" and "your account". A customer who sees the staff chrome reasonably concludes they are seeing a staff screen — and then wonders what else on it was meant for them.

That is not a styling quibble. The entire strategy rests on a customer never being able to see cost, margin or supplier. A surface that LOOKS like the internal app makes every one of those a question in the customer's mind, and one leaked screenshot becomes indistinguishable from a leaked admin screen.

SECOND, and smaller: the register is cold. "Entry", "Line", "Balance now due", a steel-grey ground and a navy bar read as administration to a fundi standing in a yard. Counter's warm paper and Shopfront's brand red both say "this is for you". This says "this is a system".

AND THE ECONOMIC ARGUMENT CUTS BOTH WAYS: one system means one blast radius. A token change to suit a customer screen now reaches forty staff screens and eight test files.

THE VERDICT ON ALL THREE

COUNTER is the better account: warm, quiet, and shaped so the balance is the first thing read and the price is a fact rather than a tag.
SHOPFRONT is the better shop: familiar, fast to learn, and unbeatable at making a tier or a bundle land.
CONSOLE is the better ledger, and the cheapest to build and keep — and it is the only one of the three that can never be allowed near a customer without solving the chrome problem first.

IF CONSOLE WERE CHOSEN, one change would be mandatory before anything else: the navy bar goes. Give the client surface its own chrome colour — the oxide, or the verdigris — keep every other token, and most of the economic argument survives while the trust problem disappears.

WHAT TO STEAL FOR COUNTER, and it is free: IBM Plex Mono for the statement's figure columns. Newsreader is the better face for a single large figure; Plex Mono is the better face for four columns that must align. Counter could use both, and the statement is where it would show.

DIRECTION C IS NOW BUILT OUT

This sketch guessed at the console vocabulary. The Console page has the real thing — every token lifted verbatim from the house design system, every house rule obeyed — with an honest account of the one thing that disqualifies it and the one change that would fix it.
Photographs — the gap in Counter, closed

THE TENSION, STATED PLAINLY

Counter's thesis is that a price is a fact on a statement, not a tag on a shelf. Photographs pull the other way. Put a rounded, shadowed thumbnail on every catalogue row and Counter quietly becomes a worse Shopfront.

But the objection to ignoring them is stronger: this is hardware. A customer needs to know whether the mabati is box profile or corrugated, which gate valve, which colour. The data already carries it — a product_images bucket, a media library, an image per VARIANT, and an image on a sourcing lead. Refusing photographs would be refusing the shop's own evidence.

SO THE RULE IS ABOUT PURPOSE, NOT QUANTITY. A photograph is EVIDENCE. It answers "is this the thing I mean", and it appears exactly where that question is live. It is absent where it is not.

Which yields the one line that keeps the language intact: photographs belong to IDENTITY, never to MONEY. None on the statement, the receipt, the account or the storekeeper's count.

TWO VIEWS, AND THE DEFAULT IS THE JOB

The honest answer to "how big should the thumbnail be" turned out to be "it depends which customer". A trade buyer reordering iron sheets does not need a picture. Somebody who cannot name the thing needs nothing else.

So the catalogue has a LIST and a GALLERY, one tap apart, and the list is the default because reordering is the job the portal exists for.

THE JUDGMENT CALL, and it is worth arguing about: the list row DOES carry a photograph, at 48px, square and ruled. Small enough that the figure on the right is still the visual anchor and the row still reads as a ledger line — but there, and useful for scanning. A rounded shadowed thumbnail at that same size would break it; the square rule is what keeps it an index card rather than a product card.

The gallery is still not cards. Each cell is a ruled print on the linen mat with its caption beneath, and the price stays in the type rather than moving into a badge.

VARIANTS ARE THE CASE THAT SETTLES IT

The data has carried an image per variant since variants existed, and the catalogue read path was already fixed once for sending the parent product's photo to every colour.

This is where photographs stop being nice and start being load-bearing: a colour named in words is a guess, a colour shown is a fact. Four 72px prints, the chosen one under a 2px ink rule, the name beneath.

And the fourth has no photograph on file — so it says so, in a dashed frame, and offers the act: ask, and the shop sends one on WhatsApp before you decide. "Not enough is an answer", applied to an image.

The filmstrip under the main photograph uses small ruled prints rather than dots. Counter has no dots; a dot tells you there are three pictures, a print tells you what the third one is.

THE PHOTOGRAPH THAT MATTERS MOST IS THE CUSTOMER'S

This is the commercial one. The strategy argued that "we do not list it" is the most valuable thing a customer can tell this shop — a free demand signal the sourcing side already knows how to turn into a product.

A photograph is how that signal actually arrives. In a hardware market the customer very often cannot name the thing, and a picture of the old one, or of something on a neighbour's site, settles the make and the size faster than any description. The sourcing_leads table already has a column for it.

So the ask leads with the camera, not the text field: "You do not have to know what it is called." The customer's photograph gets exactly the treatment ours does — 4:3, square, ruled, on the mat — because it is the same kind of object: evidence.

Captioned "only we see it", because somebody photographing a rival's site should know where it goes.

WEIGHT, WHICH IS A DESIGN DECISION HERE AND NOT AN ENGINEERING ONE

A mid-range Android on a bad line in a yard in the afternoon. The list fetches NO photographs; the gallery fetches them, and the customer chose the gallery.

That is only possible because the list was designed to work without them — the 48px frame reserves its space and draws its own rule, so nothing reflows when an image does or does not arrive. A layout that jumps when photographs land is the same defect as a figure that changes after you have read it.

STILL NOT DRAWN: the delivery photograph. The storekeeper screen already says a burst cement bag was "photographed, and the driver saw it", and there is no interface for taking it. Same component, same treatment, on the count screen — and on this session's record it would be better settled by drawing than by arguing.

A PHOTOGRAPH THAT IS A CLAIM

The storekeeper screen already said a burst cement bag was "photographed, and the driver saw it", and there was no interface for taking it. This is it, and it is the sharpest test the image rules get: a screen with NO MONEY ON IT AT ALL, where a photograph is doing nothing but being evidence.

THE PHOTOGRAPH CARRIES ITS OWN PROVENANCE. "10:31am, on DN-2419" sits under it as a caption. A picture with no time and nothing attached to it is not evidence, it is a picture — and this one will be read weeks later by two people arguing about a bag neither of them saw.

TWO ANGLES, AND THE SCREEN SAYS WHY: the bag itself and the load it came off. A close picture proves the damage; a wide one proves where it was. That is the difference between a claim that settles and one that becomes a conversation.

WHO SAW IT is the field worth the most, and it is free to fill in at this moment and expensive to prove afterwards — so the driver is a tick, already ticked, with his lorry plate under his name. "Getting the driver to see it now costs nothing. Proving it afterwards costs an argument."

DAMAGED, NOT SHORT. Forty arrived, forty counted, one unusable. Short never came; damaged came and cannot be used, and they settle against different people.

AND THE BOUNDARY IS SAID OUT LOUD: this goes to the shop and the bursar, and Peter is not agreeing to anything about money. He never sees what a bag costs and he does not need to. A grep of this artboard finds no figure with a comma in it and no currency word anywhere.

IF HE CANNOT TAKE ONE, he can still record it — and the screen says plainly that his word is taken and that a claim with a picture settles the same day. Not enough is an answer; it is just a slower one.
